newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pact reached for first Bosnian parliament session.
newsitem.headline: Pact reached for first Bosnian parliament session.

text.p: Bosnia's inter-ethnic presidency agreed on Monday to set the first postwar session of parliament for January 3, ending weeks of obstruction by Serb deputies.

Parliament was elected in OSCE-supervised elections held last September to reunite Moslem-Croat and Serb sectors of Bosnia, but has not yet convened because of manoeuvring and stalling by former combatants, mainly Serbs.

But on Monday the collective presidency, which includes Serb nationalist leader Momcilo Krajisnik, Moslem president Alija Izetbegovic and Croat representative Kresimir Zubak, announced it wanted parliament to meet on Friday.

"The Presidency calls on the House of Representatives of Bosnia ... to convene in Sarajevo on January 3 and to approve the nominations of the co-chairs of the Council of Ministers (cabinet)," it said in a statement.
The presidency said parliament's upper House of Peoples should also meet for the first time in the Serb-controlled Sarajevo suburb of Lukavica on the same day.

"The Presidency requests the Council of Ministers, after having been approved by the House of Representatives, to consider with urgency the question of a permanent arrangement on the premises, location and functioning of the common institutions of Bosnia."

One of the major reasons for prolonged delays in convening both the legislatures and presidency, whose first full session was weeks after the September 14 election, was wrangling over venues for meetings.

Parliament has never held a full session since separatist-minded Serb members boycotted an inaugural ceremony in October in Sarajevo, citing concerns over the venue and the text of an oath of allegiance to a single Bosnian state.
Serb leaders also linked their attendance to the parliament to objections over the venue for the cabinet.

Despite an agreement to alternate cabinet meetings between the country's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic, Bosnian Serbs demanded the council of ministers meet more frequently on Serb territory, or outside Sarajevo.
The capital is controlled by the federation. The Moslem-Croat entity and the Serb Republic make up what are supposed to be autonomous but not independent regions in a decentralised country.
The office of the international High Representative, charged with overseeing civilian aspects of the Bosnian peace agreement, had accused the Serbs of reneging on previous agreements.

Michael Steiner, deputy High Representative, said last week that Serb leaders in Pale, outside Sarajevo, were blocking attempts to build joint governing bodies devised to reunite the country after 3-1/2 years of war.
Similar warnings in the past from the High Representative have failed to move the ultra-nationalist Serb leadership, which advocated a separate Serb state during 43 months of war.

The Dayton peace agreement obliges the Serbs to recognise a weak central government for Bosnia, comprised of the collective presidency and inter-ethnic parliament, ruling over Moslem-Croat and Serb territories.
